## Doubly Stochastic Variational Inference

@salimbeni_doubly_2017 introduced a more elegant approach to DGP inference that avoids the mean-field approximation over layer outputs. The key insight is to use Monte Carlo estimation of the nested expectations while maintaining the exact conditional structure through the GP prior.

The variational distribution retains the form from @eq-dgp_variational_factorization:

$$
q(\{\vF^{(\ell)}, \vU^{(\ell)}\}) = \prod_{\ell=1}^{L} p(\vF^{(\ell)} \mid \vU^{(\ell)}, \vF^{(\ell-1)}) q(\vU^{(\ell)}),
$$ {#eq-dsvi_variational}

but rather than introducing additional variational parameters for $\vF^{(\ell)}$, the method propagates samples through the layers. This respects the hierarchical structure: $\vF^{(\ell)}$ is generated from $\vF^{(\ell-1)}$ via the GP conditional, with uncertainty injected only through the inducing variables $\vU^{(\ell)}$.

The ELBO decomposes over data points:

$$
\mathcal{L} = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \mathbb{E}_{q(f_i^{(L)})}[\log p(y_i \mid f_i^{(L)})] - \sum_{\ell=1}^{L} \KL(q(\vU^{(\ell)}) \| p(\vU^{(\ell)})).
$$ {#eq-dsvi_elbo}

The factorisation follows from $p(\vy \mid \vF^{(L)}) = \prod_i p(y_i \mid f_i^{(L)})$. The KL terms have closed form since both $q(\vU^{(\ell)})$ and $p(\vU^{(\ell)})$ are Gaussian (the standard Gaussian KL). The challenge lies in computing $\mathbb{E}_{q(f_i^{(L)})}[\log p(y_i \mid f_i^{(L)})]$, which requires marginalising over all intermediate layers. The distribution $q(f_i^{(L)})$ is obtained by integrating:

$$
q(f_i^{(L)}) = \int \cdots \int p(f_i^{(L)} \mid \vU^{(L)}, f_i^{(L-1)}) q(\vU^{(L)}) \cdots p(f_i^{(1)} \mid \vU^{(1)}, \vx_i) q(\vU^{(1)}) \, d\vU^{(1)} \cdots d\vU^{(L)}.
$$ {#eq-marginal_q_output}

This nested integral is analytically intractable due to the nonlinear dependence of kernel matrices on previous layer outputs.

The doubly stochastic approach estimates this expectation via Monte Carlo. For data point $\vx_i$, we construct a sample path through all layers. Starting at layer 1, the marginal distribution over $f_i^{(1)}$ given $\vx_i$ is:

$$
q(f_i^{(1)} \mid \vx_i) = \int p(f_i^{(1)} \mid \vU^{(1)}, \vx_i) q(\vU^{(1)}) \, d\vU^{(1)}.
$$ {#eq-layer1_marginal}

Since $p(f_i^{(1)} \mid \vU^{(1)}, \vx_i) = \mathcal{N}(f_i^{(1)} \mid k_i^{(1)\top} (K_{uu}^{(1)})^{-1} \vU^{(1)}, \, k_{ii}^{(1)} - k_i^{(1)\top} (K_{uu}^{(1)})^{-1} k_i^{(1)})$ and $q(\vU^{(1)}) = \mathcal{N}(\vM^{(1)}, \vS^{(1)})$, integrating out $\vU^{(1)}$ yields:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mu_i^{(1)} &= k_i^{(1)\top} (K_{uu}^{(1)})^{-1} \vM^{(1)}, \\
\sigma_i^{(1)2} &= k_{ii}^{(1)} - k_i^{(1)\top} (K_{uu}^{(1)})^{-1} (K_{uu}^{(1)} - \vS^{(1)}) (K_{uu}^{(1)})^{-1} k_i^{(1)},
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-layer1_moments}

where $k_i^{(1)} = k^{(1)}(\vx_i, \vZ^{(1)}) \in \mathbb{R}^{m_1}$ and $k_{ii}^{(1)} = k^{(1)}(\vx_i, \vx_i)$.

Sampling $f_i^{(1)} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_i^{(1)}, \sigma_i^{(1)2})$ gives a realisation of the first layer output. For subsequent layers $\ell = 2, \ldots, L$, we condition on the sampled value from the previous layer. The distribution at layer $\ell$ given sampled $f_i^{(\ell-1)}$ is:

$$
q(f_i^{(\ell)} \mid f_i^{(\ell-1)}) = \int p(f_i^{(\ell)} \mid \vU^{(\ell)}, f_i^{(\ell-1)}) q(\vU^{(\ell)}) \, d\vU^{(\ell)},
$$ {#eq-layer_conditional}

with mean and variance:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mu_i^{(\ell)} &= k^{(\ell)}(f_i^{(\ell-1)}, \vZ^{(\ell)})^\top (K_{uu}^{(\ell)})^{-1} \vM^{(\ell)}, \\
\sigma_i^{(\ell)2} &= k^{(\ell)}(f_i^{(\ell-1)}, f_i^{(\ell-1)}) - k^{(\ell)}(f_i^{(\ell-1)}, \vZ^{(\ell)})^\top (K_{uu}^{(\ell)})^{-1} (K_{uu}^{(\ell)} - \vS^{(\ell)}) (K_{uu}^{(\ell)})^{-1} k^{(\ell)}(\vZ^{(\ell)}, f_i^{(\ell-1)}).
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-layer_ell_moments}

The kernel evaluations now depend on the random variable $f_i^{(\ell-1)}$ from the previous layer, creating the propagation of uncertainty.

After sampling through all $L$ layers, we obtain $f_i^{(L)}$ and evaluate $\log p(y_i \mid f_i^{(L)})$. With $S$ independent sample paths, the Monte Carlo estimate of the ELBO is:

$$
\hat{\mathcal{L}} = \frac{n}{|\mathcal{B}|} \sum_{i \in \mathcal{B}} \frac{1}{S} \sum_{s=1}^{S} \log p(y_i \mid f_i^{(L,s)}) - \sum_{\ell=1}^{L} \KL(q(\vU^{(\ell)}) \| p(\vU^{(\ell)})),
$$ {#eq-dsvi_mc_elbo}

where $\mathcal{B} \subset \{1, \ldots, n\}$ is a minibatch and $f_i^{(L,s)}$ denotes the $s$-th sample at the final layer for point $i$. The factor $n/|\mathcal{B}|$ corrects for minibatch subsampling, ensuring the estimate remains unbiased.

The term "doubly stochastic" refers to two sources of randomness: minibatch subsampling (stochasticity over data) and Monte Carlo sampling through layers (stochasticity over latent functions). Both maintain unbiasedness of gradient estimates, which is crucial for stochastic optimisation convergence.

Gradient computation requires differentiating through the sampling operations. The reparameterisation trick [@kingma_auto-encoding_2014] makes this tractable: instead of sampling $f \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)$ directly, we write $f = \mu + \sigma\epsilon$ with $\epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0,1)$, so that gradients with respect to $\mu$ and $\sigma$ flow through the deterministic transformation while the stochastic node $\epsilon$ carries no parameters.

Computational cost per iteration is $O(|\mathcal{B}| m^2 L S)$ for forward propagation of $S$ samples through $L$ layers, plus $O(m^3 L)$ for the KL terms. Crucially, this is independent of $n$, enabling scalability to large datasets. Empirically, a single sample ($S=1$) often suffices when $|\mathcal{B}|$ is large, as averaging over many data points provides natural variance reduction.
